items.title: Michigan cold
items.body: The extra inch is on the whole driveway because this is a cold climate, not because a spec sheet said so. Freeze and thaw work on a four-inch slab. So does a 20-ton delivery truck coming in and out. The approach takes that hit first, which is why it is six inches, and the rest of the drive is still five.

items.title: The cheap inch
items.body: Most contractors pour four inches. They skip the inch because it is cheaper, on the order of $600 to $700 on an average driveway. Matt's line for it is that they are tripping over dollars to pick up pennies. If you are looking for a cheap deal, Faber Concrete is not going to be it. The bid is the best quality one, priced down the middle, with a better finish.

items.title: What is under it
items.body: We never pour over dirt. We also do not deliver sand, compact the sand, and call that a base. That shortcut saves a few hundred dollars, and sand and the soil under a slab can erode out from underneath. We take 21AA, grade the whole area, compact the whole area, and then pour. That is how it is supposed to be done, every time.

items.title: The crack you live with
items.body: A thin slab does not always fail the year it is poured. It cracks enough that you hate the driveway long before you are ready to tear it out. The finishers have been finishing concrete for more than 25 years. The finish is what you see. The inches and the 21AA are what keep you from living with that crack early.

ownerStory.label: About Us
ownerStory.quote: If you are looking for a cheap deal, we are not going to be it. We are going to be your best, highest quality bid.
ownerStory.caption: Matt Faber · Owner
paragraphs: Matt Faber owns Faber Concrete. It is a separate company on purpose. A page that sells roofs and driveways together reads like a jack of all trades, and concrete is a specialty. Fewer companies even know how to do it, and a lot of the ones who do never advertise. This site is only the slab.

We never pour a four-inch driveway. Five inches, every time, no matter the driveway, and six inches on the approach. That is an inch more than what most contractors pour, on the driveway and again where it meets the street. They skip it because it is cheaper, on the order of $600 to $700 on an average driveway. Matt tells people, when he gives the estimate, that if they are looking for a cheap deal, this is not it. The bid is the highest quality one, priced down the middle, with a superior finish.

The extra inch is there because Michigan is cold, and because a 20-ton delivery truck uses a driveway. A thinner slab can crack enough that you hate it long before you are ready to replace it. That is the expensive failure. It is not always bad enough to tear out this year. It is bad enough that you live with a driveway you do not like.

Thickness does not save a slab on the wrong ground. We never pour over dirt. We never compact a layer of sand and call it a base. That sand shortcut saves a few hundred dollars, and the ground under the slab can erode out. We grade 21AA across the whole area, compact it, then form, then pour. The finishers have been finishing concrete for more than 25 years. After the site look, Matt writes a contract, not only an estimate.
